Senses.Note: The common parallel begins with either “form an intention” or “raise the mind” , followed by “at once err” . The entry does not infer why moving thought deviates; it records the phrase's question-answer and verdict deployments and the texts' explicit dead-water, wood-and-earth, and eyebrow replies.

Senses.Explanation: “Stir a thought and at once deviate” functions as a compact verdict, but the records immediately deny that mere nonmovement or dead-water stillness resolves it. Literally, “stir a thought and at once deviate.” The phrase's Zen-specific deployment is a compact verdict and answer, frequently paired with “form an intention and at once err” , but the corpus explicitly refuses to turn its negative wording into mere mental stillness. Huangbo says, “it is just this; stir a thought and at once deviate” , then compares what he has described to measureless space. Linji pairs “form an intention and at once err” with the headword and immediately continues with the person who understands not being apart from what is before the eyes . Shimen Cizhao quotes the pair and adds: “not intending and not moving, one is doing business in dead water” . Huanglong Huinan gives the parallel correction: “not intending and not moving is no different from wood and earth; a traveling monk must obtain a turning phrase” . In direct questions, Tianyin answers “What is the body of things?” with the phrase, while Linye Qi answers “How, finally, should one head toward it?” with it and answers the follow-up “what about when thought does not move?” with “the eyebrows are above the eyes” . The record thus bends an ordinary warning about a wayward thought into a portable Chan verdict while its own corrections exclude “do not think” as a complete gloss.
